opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the interesting thing is that a lot of the ideas behind Lakebase carry over pretty naturally to sandboxes. With Lakebase, the core insight was separating storage from compute for an operational database. You keep the durable state in cheap, scalable object storage, and the compute layer becomes something you can spin up, scale down to zero, branch, and throw away. That's what lets you do things like instantly fork a database for a test or for an agent to experiment on, without copying all the data.

When you look at what agents need from a compute sandbox, it's surprisingly similar. An agent wants an environment where it can try something, run code, install packages, mess with files, and if it goes wrong, just roll back or branch off and try a different path. And you want to run many of these in parallel, cheaply, and have them start up really fast. So the same primitives apply: copy-on-write storage, fast snapshots, branching, and compute that's ephemeral and elastic rather than a long-lived VM you're paying for all the time.

So the way we think about it is, the sandbox's state, the file system, maybe the memory snapshot, should live in a layer that's versioned and branchable, just like the database pages in Lakebase. Then compute attaches to a particular version, does its work, and you can checkpoint it again. That gives you really nice properties for agents: you can explore a tree of possibilities, you can reproduce exactly what happened for debugging or evaluation, and you get governance, because everything the agent touched is tracked in the same platform as your data.

There are differences, of course. Databases have very structured state and well-understood access patterns, whereas a general-purpose sandbox is running arbitrary code, so isolation and security matter a lot more, and startup latency for a full environment is a harder problem than attaching to a Postgres page server. But a lot of the engineering we did for fast branching and scale-to-zero turned out to be directly reusable. And I think long term, you want the agent's data and the agent's compute environment to be closely connected, so it can work on real enterprise data safely, and that's really where having both in one system pays off.

r001.rationale: The response describes reusing Lakebase’s separation of storage and compute, but does not say the database is removed from the architecture to build the sandbox.

r002.rationale: It does not mention local persistence preventing libraries from needing to be reinstalled.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Neon or explain that storage-compute separation removes the need for persistent local disk.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of my favorite things we've done recently, because it came out of a problem we didn't originally set out to solve. Lakebase started as a serverless Postgres for the lakehouse. The core idea was separating storage from compute, keeping the data in object storage, and then being able to spin up a database instance in well under a second, branch it, snapshot it, throw it away, all of that. And a lot of that engineering was motivated by agents, because agents need lots of cheap, short-lived, isolated state.

What we realized pretty quickly is that the same properties you want for a database that an agent is going to hammer on are the properties you want for the compute the agent runs in. If an agent is going to write code and execute it, you want that environment to start fast, you want it fully isolated so one agent can't step on another or on production, and you want to be able to checkpoint it and fork it. So if an agent goes down a bad path, you can roll back to the state before that step, or you can fork ten copies and try ten things in parallel. That's exactly the copy-on-write, branch-and-restore model we built for Lakebase storage, just applied to a filesystem and a process rather than a Postgres page store.

So architecturally we reused a lot. The control plane that schedules and scales database instances is basically the same thing scheduling sandboxes. The separation of durable state in object storage from ephemeral compute means the sandbox itself is disposable, which is what makes it safe. And the branching layer gives you this nice property where state is cheap to copy, so you stop thinking about one environment per agent and start thinking about environments as something you create per step, per attempt.

The other thing I'd say is that putting them together matters more than either one alone. An agent that's doing real work usually needs code execution and some kind of transactional state at the same time, and having both come from the same platform, with the same governance and the same identity model, means the agent is operating inside the same permissions a user would have. That's really the piece enterprises care about. The fast cold start is fun to demo, but the reason people can actually deploy this is that the sandbox and the data both inherit the access controls that already exist in the lakehouse.

r001.rationale: The response says Lakebase’s copy-on-write model is applied to a filesystem and process, but does not identify removing the database from the architecture as the adaptation.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss local persistence or avoiding library reinstalls.

r003.rationale: It describes separating durable object-storage state from ephemeral compute, but does not explain that this removes the need for persistent local disk.

astra-6.text:
I think the key idea is separating the lifetime of the compute from the lifetime of the state. With Lakebase, you want to be able to start compute quickly, stop it when it’s idle, and preserve the data independently. For a compute sandbox, you want a similar experience: spin up an environment, run some code, and then tear down the compute without necessarily losing everything you’ve done.

So I’d think about reusing that architectural pattern, rather than treating a sandbox as a database. What state needs to persist? How do you snapshot it, and how do you create a new environment from that snapshot cheaply? That’s particularly useful for agents, where you might want to try several approaches from the same starting point.

The additional challenge is that a sandbox executes arbitrary code. You need strong isolation and controls around what it can access. So the storage and compute separation is a useful foundation, but the execution boundary needs its own design.

r002.rationale: It discusses preserving sandbox state but does not explain that local persistence avoids reinstalling libraries.

sol-6.1.text:
The key idea is to separate the lifetime of the compute from the lifetime of the state. With Lakebase, you want to be able to start a Postgres instance quickly, stop it when it’s idle, and bring it back without losing the database. A compute sandbox has a very similar requirement: you want an isolated environment that you can create quickly, use for a task, and then suspend or discard.

So you can apply the same architectural ideas around durable storage, snapshots, and cheap clones. For example, an agent could start from an environment with its dependencies already installed, make changes, and preserve a checkpoint without keeping the compute running the whole time.

The part you have to add is the execution boundary. A sandbox runs arbitrary code, so isolation, resource limits, and control over network and credential access become central. The storage architecture gives you a useful foundation, but you still need to design that execution layer carefully.

r001.rationale: It discusses separating compute lifetime from state and using durable storage, but never says to remove the database from the Lakebase architecture.

r002.rationale: It says dependencies can already be installed in a starting environment, but does not explain that local persistence avoids reinstalling libraries on each use.

r003.rationale: It describes durable storage and snapshots, but does not identify Neon's separation of storage from compute or explain that this removes the need for persistent local disk.
